n: On the mountain the Lord begins giving Moses detailed instructions for the tabernacle — a portable temple where He would dwell among His people. Chapters 25–31 record these instructions.

f.g: Spoke.

n: The materials were to come only from willing givers. God wanted offerings given freely from the heart, not taxes forced from the people.
The list of materials begins with metals. Much of this wealth likely came from the Egyptians when Israel left Egypt.

f.g: Really bronze or copper; brass as we know it was not yet in use.

n: Next come costly dyed yarns, fine linen, and goat hair for the curtains and priestly clothing. Blue, purple, and scarlet dyes were expensive marks of royalty.

f.g: A blue-violet dye made from sea snails.
Finely woven Egyptian linen.
Woven into tough, dark tent cloth.

n: Leather coverings and a durable desert wood complete the structural materials.

f.g: Hebrew taḥash; uncertain — possibly fine leather or the hide of a sea animal such as a dugong.
Acacia, a hard, lasting wood that grows in the Sinai desert.

n: Olive oil fueled the lamps, and spices were blended into sacred anointing oil and incense.
Precious stones were needed for the high priest’s ephod and breastplate, described in chapter 28.

f.g: An apron-like sacred vestment worn by the high priest.

n: Here is the heart of it all: God wants a holy place so that He can live among His people. The tabernacle, and later temples, exist so heaven and earth can meet.

f.g: Holy place.

f.w: that I may dwell among them

n: Everything must be built exactly according to the heavenly pattern God shows Moses. Hebrews teaches that the earthly tabernacle was a copy of heavenly realities.

f.g: Hebrew mishkan — dwelling place.

n: The most sacred object comes first: the ark, a chest of acacia wood about 3¾ by 2¼ by 2¼ feet. It would sit in the innermost room, the Holy of Holies.

f.g: A chest or box (a different Hebrew word from Noah’s ark).
A cubit was about 18 inches, the length from elbow to fingertip.

n: The ark was covered inside and out with pure gold, with a gold molding around the top. Ordinary wood made glorious by gold has been seen by some as an image of humanity joined with divinity.

f.g: A decorative rim or molding.

n: Four gold rings, two on each side, were attached at the ark’s feet for carrying.

f.g: Mold from molten metal.

n: The carrying poles were made of acacia wood covered with gold.

f.g: Poles.

n: The poles slid through the rings so the ark could be carried — it was never to be touched directly.

f.g: Carried.

n: The poles were to stay in the rings permanently, ready to travel whenever God’s presence led Israel onward.

f.w: they shall not be taken from it

n: Inside the ark went “the testimony” — the stone tablets of the law, God’s covenant witness. Later a pot of manna and Aaron’s budding rod were kept with it.

f.g: The tablets bearing the Ten Commandments, which testified to the covenant.

n: A solid gold lid, the “mercy seat,” covered the ark. Once a year the high priest sprinkled atoning blood on it — a powerful symbol of Christ’s Atonement.

f.g: Hebrew kapporet, related to kipper, “to atone” or “cover”; the place of atonement.

n: Two golden cherubim were hammered out of the same piece of gold as the lid, one at each end.

f.g: Cherubim are heavenly beings who guard God’s holy presence (the KJV adds an extra English plural -s).
Hammered from one piece of metal.

n: The cherubim formed one piece with the mercy seat, standing at its two ends.
Their wings stretched upward and over the lid, and their faces looked down toward the mercy seat, as if in reverent attention to the place of atonement.

f.w: stretch forth their wings on high

n: The mercy seat rested on top of the ark, covering the tablets of the law. Symbolically, mercy covers the law.
This is why the ark mattered: there, between the cherubim above the mercy seat, God would meet and speak with Moses. The place of atonement is the place of communion with God.

f.w: there I will meet with thee

f.g: Speak intimately.

n: Next, a table about 3 feet long, 1½ feet wide, and 2¼ feet high was to stand in the Holy Place, the first room of the tabernacle.
Like the ark, the table was covered with gold and edged with a gold molding.
A rim about a handbreadth (roughly 3 inches) wide ran around it, also trimmed with gold, perhaps to keep items from sliding off.

f.g: The width of a palm, about 3 inches.

n: Gold rings were attached at the table’s four legs for carrying.
The rings sat near the rim to hold the carrying poles.

f.g: Next to, alongside.

n: The table’s poles were also gold-covered acacia wood, so it could travel with Israel.
Pure gold dishes, ladles, jars, and bowls were made for the table, likely for incense and drink offerings.

f.g: Small ladles or pans, perhaps for incense.
Better, “to pour with” — vessels for drink offerings.

n: Bread was always kept on the table in God’s presence — twelve loaves, one for each tribe. Jesus called Himself “the bread of life.”

f.g: “Bread of the Presence” — bread set before the Lord.
Always.

n: A lampstand of pure gold was hammered out of a single piece, with its base, shaft, branches, and decorations all of one piece.

f.g: Hebrew menorah — a lampstand holding oil lamps, not candles.
Knobs; round ornamental buds.

n: Three branches curved out from each side of the central shaft, making seven lamps in all.
Each branch was decorated with three cups shaped like almond blossoms. The almond is the first tree to bloom in spring, suggesting life and watchfulness.
The central shaft had four almond-shaped cups with their buds and blossoms.
A bud-shaped knob sat beneath each pair of branches where they joined the shaft.
Everything was to be one hammered piece of pure gold — no joints or seams. The lampstand looked like a golden flowering tree, which some connect with the tree of life.
Seven lamps sat atop the branches, lighting the area in front of it. Since the Holy Place had no windows, this was its only light — a symbol of God’s light and of Christ, the Light of the World.
Even the wick-trimmers and trays for burnt wicks were made of pure gold.

f.g: Snuffers or wick-trimmers.
Trays to hold trimmed wicks.

n: The lampstand and its tools took a full talent of gold — about 75 pounds (34 kg) — showing how precious it was.

f.g: A large unit of weight, roughly 75 pounds.

n: God repeats the key instruction: build everything exactly according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Temples follow revealed patterns, not human design.
